title: Kinesiology and Combat Choreography in Grappler Baki
summary: Part 2 of NH's Grappler Baki analysis, on how Itagaki conveys movement in still panels. He describes three tiers: movement execution (the aftermath of a blow), movement prediction (linked panels that freeze time), and movement suspension (the iconic frozen mid-action frame). Ideally they are mixed about 60/20/20 and channel violence into narrative.
claims: Manga runs at roughly 4-5 frames per second, yet good artists convey complex human motion; Itagaki has mastered it despite questionable art and narrative tendencies
Movement in Baki is shown in three tiers that tell a visual story without dialogue
Tier one, movement execution, shows a blow just landed or ending, using blur, impact marks, foot position and center of gravity; it often links action scenes and gives the fight room to breathe
Tier two, movement prediction, uses several causally linked panels with the main action in one frame, showing past, present and future of a motion
Overusing blur makes fights hard to follow; drawing the striking body part keeps the action clear
Tier three, movement suspension, is the iconic frozen mid-action frame (Goku's Kamehameha, Luffy's punch, Jack's uppercut); overused or used without lead-up it looks choppy
Mixing suspension with the other two tiers at roughly 60/20/20 produces iconic, memorable fights
Even fight build-ups without punches show motion, as waves of animosity seem to bend space
Anyone can draw stick figures and red ink, but using violence to tell a story through anatomical movement is a craft Itagaki has raised to an art
